description: A trend detective for your town.
summary: People hear that their town is "getting hotter" or "getting wetter", but rarely see the evidence. Since 1981 is a free web tool that lets anyone pick a place (any of the Philippines' 1,644 cities and municipalities, or any coordinates on Earth) and a climate variable, and get an honest verdict from 45 years of NASA POWER data: is it really changing, by how much, and how sure can we be? It builds yearly averages, measures the rate of change with the Theil-Sen slope, and tests significance with the Mann-Kendall test. Every claim shows its evidence. It also tells you when not to trust a trend. In Davao, rainfall rose significantly, but most of the rise happens in one jump in 1999–2000, a sign that a change in the observations feeding NASA's model may be involved. The site flags this beside the verdict.
details:
What it does. People hear that their town is "getting hotter" or "getting wetter", but rarely see the evidence. Since 1981 lets anyone pick a place (any of the Philippines' 1,644 cities and municipalities, or any coordinates on Earth) and a variable (temperature or rainfall), and get an honest verdict from 45 years of NASA POWER data: is it really changing, by how much, and how sure can we be?

How it works. One request to the NASA POWER monthly point API returns 1981–2025 temperature (T2M) and rainfall (PRECTOTCORR) for the chosen point. The site keeps only complete years and averages them. It measures the rate of change with the Theil-Sen slope: the median slope between every pair of years, so one odd year cannot swing it. It then tests significance with a two-sided Mann-Kendall test, corrected for ties. The verdict is in plain words: Significant trend (p < 0.05), Possible trend (0.05–0.10), or No significant trend yet, which is treated as a real answer. Every verdict shows its evidence: the slope, p-value, years used and source. There is also a chart, a data table, the four method steps with live numbers, CSV downloads and a shareable link.

A detective, not a calculator. Manila is warming by +0.13 °C per decade (p = 0.002), Baguio by +0.18 °C (p < 0.001). Davao's rainfall is up +0.73 mm/day per decade (p < 0.001), but most of that rise is one jump: the yearly mean goes from 3.68 mm/day before 1999 to 5.84 mm/day after 2000. A shift like this can come from a change in the observations feeding NASA's model, so the site flags it beside the verdict. It tells you when not to trust a trend.

Impact. Students and the public can check climate claims about their own town in one click, in language a senior high school student understands, with the limits stated openly: model reanalysis rather than station data, a straight-line summary, and a trend is not a cause.

Validity. The slope and Mann-Kendall results were independently checked against the Python package pymannkendall and match to 3 decimals for all three case files.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Chart.js; no backend and no user data collected; Python for the place directory and the statistics check; accessible (WCAG AA, keyboard, data table) and phone-friendly; hosted on GitHub Pages.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources)
